summary: Defines a certificate profile for SEcure Neighbor Discovery based on resource certificates, with extended key usage values for SEND. SEND uses certificates to authorize routers. It updates RFC 3971.

eli5.summary: On a network, devices announce who they are. SEND uses digital ID cards to check that a router is allowed to act as a router. This defines what is on that card.

questions: what is secure neighbor discovery certificate profile
how does send use rpki certificates
subtitle: How routers, proxies and address owners prove their right to speak in IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, using RPKI certificates.

tldr.problem: SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) uses X.509 certificates to authorize routers, but the original profile did not say why a certificate was issued or tie it to the global address-allocation PKI.
tldr.mechanism: SEND certificates must follow the RPKI resource certificate profile and carry one of four extended key usage values that name the role: router, proxied router, owner or proxied owner.
tldr.outcome: Hosts can check both that a certificate covers the right IPv6 prefix and that it was issued for the role the Neighbor Discovery message needs. It updates RFC 3971.

today: RFC 6494 is a Proposed Standard from February 2012 that updates RFC 3971. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why SEND Needs a Certificate Profile
sections.content:
SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND, RFC 3971) uses X.509v3 certificates with the RFC 3779 extension for IPv6 addresses to certify that a router is authorized to advertise an IPv6 prefix for Neighbor Discovery.

This document supersedes the profile for Router Authorization Certificates in RFC 3971. Certificates used in SEND, whether by routers, proxies or address owners, MUST conform to the new profile and MAY also conform to the original one.

The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) is the global PKI that attests to the allocation of IP address space. It matches the centralized model of RFC 3971, so SEND uses the RPKI certificate profile and the certificate validation of RFC 6487.
sections.eli5: Routers carry ID cards to prove they are allowed to do their job. This RFC says the cards must follow the same rules as the worldwide registry of who owns which addresses.

sections.title: The SEND Certificate Profile
sections.content:
SEND certificates MUST comply with the RPKI resource profile in RFC 6487. They MUST include the IP Address Delegation extension from RFC 3779, with at least one address block for the IPv6 address family (AFI=0002). They MUST NOT have more than one such extension.

RFC 3971 defined an Unconstrained category of certificates that had either a null prefix or no prefix extension. Under the RPKI profile the prefix extension is mandatory and the null prefix must be validated. A certificate can still inherit its parent's prefix or range by using the inherit element for the IPv6 AFI.

So this document adds text to Section 7.3 of RFC 3971: operators who do not want to constrain routers to particular subnet prefixes should give them certificates containing inherit for the IPv6 AFI.
sections.eli5: Each card must list which addresses it covers. If you do not want to list them one by one, the card can say "same as my boss's card".

sections.title: Deployment Models and Trust Anchors
sections.content:
RFC 3971 described centralized and decentralized models, which differ in having one trust anchor or many. This document adds two models based on where SEND is deployed instead.

  • The local model confines SEND to one administrative domain. It can run without RPKI deployment higher up, uses local trust anchors (islands of trust) and may include Unique Local Addresses (RFC 4193).
  • The public model ties SEND to RPKI deployment (RFC 6480). Trust anchor material may belong to another administrative domain such as an RIR, NIR or ISP. It is a global model suitable for mobile users.

The models are not exclusive. In one hybrid, global unicast addresses are certified under the global RPKI while ULAs are certified under local trust anchors.

Relying parties such as end hosts MUST be configured with one or more trust anchors. In the local model, a trust anchor whose address extension holds the prefix ::/0 avoids needing new trust anchor material when renumbering. Moving from the local to the public model, however, requires distributing new trust anchor material.
sections.eli5: You can run your own small ID office just for your building, or use the big worldwide one. You can also mix both, but if you switch you must hand out new trusted stamps.

sections.title: Extended Key Usage Values
sections.content:
The extended key usage (EKU) extension lists purposes for which a key may be used. RFC 6487 makes it optional for end-entity certificates, but it MUST be present when issuing end-entity certificates for SEND. If present it MUST be non-critical.

This document defines four KeyPurposeId values:

  • id-kp-sendRouter allows a router to generate Router Advertisement and Redirect messages for prefixes covered by the certificate.
  • id-kp-sendProxiedRouter allows a proxy to proxy Router Advertisement and Redirect messages for those prefixes.
  • id-kp-sendOwner allows a node to use addresses covered by the certificate: assign them to an interface, send and receive traffic, and send or respond to NS, NA and RS messages for them.
  • id-kp-sendProxiedOwner allows a proxy to proxy NS, NA and RS messages for those addresses.

Additional values may be specified in Standards Track documents.
sections.eli5: Each ID card has a job label: router, router's helper, address owner, or owner's helper. The label says exactly what the card holder may do.

sections.title: Validation and Revocation
sections.content:
A host MUST run the certificate validation method of RFC 6487. This updates Section 6.3.1 of RFC 3971 with new checks and no conflict. The host MUST also verify that the KeyPurposeId matching the Neighbor Discovery message type is present.

Relying parties MUST require the EKU extension and MAY require a particular value. If a certificate lists several values, they need only recognize the one they require. They MUST reject certificates without at least one SEND KeyPurposeId, even if anyExtendedKeyUsage is present.

RPKI requires Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs), and the host obtains the CRLs it needs. A host MAY use OCSP, but SHOULD NOT assume certificates include an OCSP server URI, since OCSP services are not required by RFC 6484.
sections.eli5: The host checks the card is real, not cancelled, and has the right job label for what the sender is trying to do. A card with no SEND job label is turned away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The certification authority must insert the correct EKU values in every certificate it issues. Wrong values can make a relying party reject a good certificate or accept one that should be rejected.

Because a SEND certificate says its subject may play a given role, incorrect EKU values can enable some of the attacks SEND was meant to prevent. For example, a malicious host that obtains a certificate authorizing it as a router for a prefix could masquerade as that router and attract traffic from local nodes.

IANA considerations are limited to object identifiers: the EKUs and the ASN.1 module identifier are registered in an arc delegated to the PKIX Working Group.
sections.eli5: If someone hands out a router card by mistake, a trickster can pretend to be a router. So whoever prints the cards must label them correctly.
